cards.front: Why is oral bioavailability usually less than 100%?
cards.back: Incomplete absorption from the gut, plus loss from first-pass metabolism in the gut wall or liver, or excretion in bile. IV dosing gives 100% by definition.

cards.front: What is bioequivalence?
cards.back: Pharmaceutical equivalents contain the same active ingredient in the same strength, dosage form and route. Two such products are bioequivalent when the rate and extent of bioavailability of the active drug do not differ significantly under suitable, identical test conditions. Equal drug content alone does not guarantee this (formulation affects dissolution), which matters for narrow-margin drugs such as digoxin.

cards.front: At what pH is a weak acid 50% ionised, and what does a 1-unit change in pH do?
cards.back: At pH equal to pKa. Each 1-unit change in pH alters the ionised to unionised ratio tenfold.

cards.front: What is ion trapping?
cards.back: A weak electrolyte crossing a membrane becomes ionised on the far side, cannot diffuse back, and so accumulates there. Example: unionised aspirin enters gastric mucosal cells (pH about 7) and is trapped.

cards.front: Why are acidic drugs excreted faster in alkaline urine?
cards.back: They stay ionised in alkaline urine and cannot back-diffuse across the renal tubular epithelium. Acidifying urine speeds the excretion of basic drugs by the same logic.

cards.front: How do facilitated diffusion and primary active transport differ?
cards.back: Facilitated diffusion is passive, follows the concentration gradient and needs no energy. Primary active transport uses ATP hydrolysis (ABC transporters) to move the solute against its gradient, usually out of the cell.

cards.front: Which efflux transporter is encoded by MDR1, and where does it limit drug entry?
cards.back: P-glycoprotein (ABCB1). It limits absorption from the gut and entry into the brain, testes and foetus, and promotes biliary and renal elimination.

cards.front: Why can quinidine or verapamil raise digoxin levels?
cards.back: Both inhibit the efflux pump P-glycoprotein. Less P-gp efflux in the gut epithelium raises digoxin's oral bioavailability. Quinidine also cuts digoxin's renal and biliary clearance (again via P-gp) and displaces it from tissue binding sites, nearly doubling its plasma level.

cards.front: Define apparent volume of distribution and give its formula.
cards.back: The hypothetical volume into which the total amount of drug in the body would have to be dispersed to give the measured plasma concentration. Vd = amount of drug in body / plasma concentration.

cards.front: Why does a large volume of distribution make haemodialysis ineffective?
cards.back: Most of the drug sits in tissues, so very little is in plasma at any time to be cleared by dialysis. Highly protein-bound drugs are also poorly removed.

cards.front: What is redistribution, and why does a single dose of thiopentone act only briefly?
cards.back: Highly lipid-soluble drugs first enter well-perfused organs such as brain, then move to muscle and fat as plasma levels fall. Brain levels drop, so the action ends within minutes.

cards.front: What makes the blood-brain barrier, and where is it deficient?
cards.back: Tight junctions between capillary endothelial cells plus a glial investment, with lipoidal limits on entry and efflux pumps. It is deficient at the chemoreceptor trigger zone and some periventricular sites, which is why emetics can act there.

cards.front: Short note: Bioavailability and factors affecting it

points: Fraction of the dose reaching systemic circulation unchanged
Estimated from the plasma concentration-time curve (area under curve) or urinary excretion
IV dose gives F = 1
Disintegration and dissolution rate
Particle size, crystal form and excipients
Manufacturing process (e.g. compression force)
Incomplete absorption; first-pass metabolism in gut wall and liver
P-glycoprotein efflux
Food, gastric emptying, drug interactions
Matters most for poorly soluble drugs and those with narrow safety margins (digoxin, oral anticoagulants)
Bioequivalence required when switching brands or generics

cards.front: Short note: Apparent volume of distribution (Vd)

points: Vd = amount of drug in body / plasma concentration
A calculated, not anatomical, volume
Small Vd: drug confined to plasma (e.g. highly protein-bound warfarin)
Vd near extracellular water: poorly lipid-soluble drugs (e.g. aminoglycosides)
Large Vd: extensive tissue binding or sequestration (e.g. digoxin)
Lipid solubility, pKa, plasma protein binding, tissue affinity
Fat to lean mass ratio, age, sex
Disease: heart failure, uraemia, cirrhosis
Loading dose = Vd x target concentration
Estimating total drug amount in body
Dialysis removes little when Vd is large

cards.front: Short note: Plasma protein binding

points: Albumin binds mainly acidic drugs and is the more important site
Alpha-1 acid glycoprotein binds mainly basic drugs
Bound drug stays in vessels, so Vd is small
Bound fraction acts as a reservoir; only free drug is active and eliminated
Long duration when clearance depends on free fraction
Drugs competing for the same binding site can displace each other
Usually transient and clinically minor unless tissue binding or clearance also changes
Drugs with different binding sites do not displace each other
Hypoalbuminaemia raises free fraction (phenytoin)
Uraemia reduces binding; pregnancy and inflammation alter alpha-1 acid glycoprotein

cards.front: Short note: Blood-brain barrier

points: Capillary endothelium with tight junctions and no large paracellular gaps
Glial investment; blood-CSF barrier at the choroid plexus
Lipid-soluble drugs cross; nonlipid drugs (e.g. streptomycin) are excluded
Efflux transporters (P-gp, OATP) actively expel many drugs
Enzymes such as MAO limit entry of monoamines
Chemoreceptor trigger zone and periventricular regions (anterior hypothalamus)
Inflamed meninges or brain are more permeable
Exit from CNS depends on CSF bulk flow, not lipid solubility
Levodopa crosses the barrier, dopamine does not (Parkinsonism)

cards.front: Short note: Factors affecting oral absorption

points: Aqueous solubility, dissolution rate and particle size
Ionisation (pKa) and lipid solubility; highly ionised drugs (gentamicin, neostigmine) are poorly absorbed
Stability in gastric acid or digestive enzymes
Gastric emptying; food usually dilutes the drug and delays absorption (exception: fatty food increases lumefantrine absorption)
Large absorptive surface of the small intestine
Motility changes (anticholinergics slow, metoclopramide speeds)
P-glycoprotein pumps absorbed drug back into the lumen (digoxin, ciclosporin); inhibitors raise and inducers lower bioavailability
First-pass loss in the gut wall
Complex formation (tetracyclines with calcium in milk, iron, antacids)
Mucosal damage by some drugs (neomycin, methotrexate)

Saturable, competitively inhibited, Michaelis-Menten kinetics
Endocytosis and exocytosis for large molecules

Drug interactions at transporters
Genetic polymorphism altering transporter density or affinity
Tissue-specific distribution via specialised transporters

points: Absorption: movement of drug from site of administration into circulation
Both extent and rate matter
Aqueous solubility and dissolution
Concentration at the site and area of absorbing surface
Vascularity and blood flow at the absorbing site
Lipid solubility and ionisation (pH-partition)

Small intestine is the main site for nearly all drugs because of its large surface area
Particle size, gastric emptying, food effects, P-gp efflux, gut-wall metabolism

Topical absorption depends on lipid solubility; rubbing, an oily base and occlusion increase it
Disintegration, dissolution and excipients

Definition and formula
Small, intermediate and large Vd and their meanings

cards.front: Passive diffusion: what decides its rate?
cards.text: Lipid-soluble drugs cross membranes by passive diffusion, at a rate proportional to their {{lipid:water partition coefficient}} and the concentration gradient.

cards.front: Classify: carrier-mediated transport
cards.text: Facilitated diffusion needs {{no energy}}; primary active transport uses {{ATP}} through ABC transporters; symport and antiport use a {{Na+}} gradient and are secondary active.

cards.front: Plasma protein binding
cards.text: Acidic drugs mainly bind {{albumin}}; basic drugs mainly bind {{alpha-1 acid glycoprotein}}.

cards.front: Tissue storage of drugs
cards.text: Tetracyclines accumulate in {{bone and teeth}}, digoxin in {{skeletal muscle}}, and iodine in the {{thyroid}}.

cards.front: Site of absorption by ionisation
cards.text: Weak acids such as {{aspirin}} are largely unionised in gastric acid and can be absorbed from the {{stomach}}; weak bases such as {{morphine}} are ionised there and are absorbed only on reaching the {{duodenum}}. Even so, the {{small intestine}} is the main site of absorption for both because of its large surface area.

cards.front: Short note: Clinical significance of body pH in drug pharmacokinetics

points: Most drugs are weak acids or weak bases; their ionisation depends on pH relative to pKa
Only the unionised form crosses lipid membranes readily
An ionised drug becomes trapped on the side of the membrane where it is ionised
Stomach pH is about 1.9 to 3; small intestine pH about 7.5 to 8
Weak acids such as aspirin stay unionised in the stomach and are absorbed there
Weak bases such as atropine are ionised in the stomach and absorbed in the intestine
Breast milk and aqueous humour can trap drugs because their pH differs from blood
Basic drugs reach higher concentration inside cells, where pH is slightly lower than plasma
Weak acids are excreted faster in alkaline urine
Weak bases are excreted faster in acidic urine
Urine pH is changed clinically to speed up excretion in poisoning
Aspirin overdose: sodium bicarbonate alkalinises urine and so increases clearance
Acidosis pushes weak acids into tissues, while acidic urine lets them be reabsorbed
Ion trapping of aspirin may add to gastric mucosal damage

cards.front: Short note: Physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modelling

points: Model in which real tissues or organs are compartments linked by blood flow
Predicts the time course of drug disposition throughout the body
Systemic exposure and tissue distribution of a drug
Effect of changes in physiological or drug-dependent parameters
Pravastatin: OATP1B1 activity mainly changes myopathy risk, with little effect on efficacy
MRP2 and BCRP activity mainly changes efficacy rather than side effects
Sensitivity analysis shows which parameter most changes efficacy or toxicity
Concentration-time data are fitted to a model, ideally a physiologically based one
Fitted parameters are used to adjust the dose to reach a target concentration
